figures.caption: Text blocks, pp. 2-3 (section 3): kappa = 0.5 compressed from phi = 0.795 to 0.915; global stress close to 0 MPa then increasing from the jamming point, phi_j = 0.84, coordination slightly above 3; specific contact length l = <l_contact/perimeter> (contacts with particles or system boundaries) increases linearly with phi, not in agreement with the Hertz contact law in 2D, not surprising since soft particles are far from the small deformation assumption; mean von Mises strain of soft particles decreases parabolically; asphericity gently increases then sharply rises after phi = 0.88 (defined as a ratio between actual area and area deduced from the perimeter); phi = 0.88 is also the maximum of the total void area.

figures.caption: Text blocks, pp. 3-4: first invariant of the strain fields at phi = 0.89 (C for soft, infinitesimal strain for rigid); high strain chains with clear areas near contact points in soft particles; rigid-particle patterns show that the imaging method is not accurate enough (stiffness ratio covers several orders of magnitude; deformation almost exclusively carried by soft particles; lines = speed inhomogeneities of the imaging); PDF of |C| in soft particles: Gaussian around 1 when gently squeezed, broader and slightly shifted to the left when loaded, exponential tail with a coefficient decreasing with phi when dense, reminiscent of force PDFs of rigid granular systems [25] and unchanged from purely soft systems [13]; standard deviation of C rises rapidly right after jamming for kappa = 0.2 and less rapidly for kappa = 0.8.

figures.label: eq-conclusion
figures.caption: Text blocks, p. 4 (section 4, Conclusion): measurement of all mechanical and geometrical observables from the displacement field at the particle scale for bidimensional systems under uniaxial compression; jamming at a packing fraction and coordination close to purely rigid systems; average von Mises strain in soft particles decreases with the exact same tendency as the global stress increases; since rigid particle deformation is negligible this suggests that rigid particles do not carry more load than the soft ones, the loading seems to be balanced; stress vs packing fraction similar to a recent numerical study [14]; exponential tail; standard deviation rises faster with more rigid particles; outlook to breakable and polydisperse (size, shape, material) particles under different loading geometries.
